clinicalContext: Intubated ARDS patient (PBW 60 kg) on VC 480 mL (8 mL/kg PBW), PEEP 8, Pplat 34 cmH2O, driving pressure 26 cmH2O. SpO2 91%.
learnerInput: I need to reduce tidal volume to 360 mL (6 mL/kg PBW) because plateau pressure is 34 cmH2O, exceeding the safe limit of 30 cmH2O and driving pressure is excessively high at 26 cmH2O.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Lung protective ventilation targets Vt 4-8 mL/kg PBW to maintain Pplat <= 30 cmH2O and driving pressure <= 14-15 cmH2O to prevent volutrauma and barotrauma.

clinicalContext: Asthmatic on VC with high Ppeak (42 cmH2O) and normal Pplat (18 cmH2O). Inspiratory flow 60 L/min.
learnerInput: The elevated peak pressure with normal plateau indicates high airway resistance rather than low lung compliance. I should treat with inhaled bronchodilators and check for circuit secretions.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Ppeak - Pplat gradient reflects resistive pressure drop across conducting airways; normal Pplat confirms normal respiratory system compliance.

clinicalContext: COPD patient on PSV 14/5 with frequent delayed cycling into expiration; flow-time curve shows prolonged inspiratory flow tails.
learnerInput: The patient has increased airway resistance prolonging the time constant. I should increase the expiratory trigger sensitivity (cycling-off threshold) from 25% to 40% to prevent delayed cycling and air trapping.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: High expiratory time constants in obstructive lung disease cause inspiratory flow to decay slowly; raising cycling-off % terminates inspiration sooner.

clinicalContext: Severe ARDS patient with PaO2/FiO2 ratio 85 mmHg despite PEEP 14 and lung-protective Vt. Neuromuscular blockade started.
learnerInput: For severe ARDS with P/F < 100 refractory to initial lung-protective settings, prone positioning for at least 16 hours is indicated to improve V/Q matching and reduce dorsal alveolar collapse.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Prone positioning promotes more uniform pleural pressure distribution and dorsal alveolar recruitment in severe ARDS.

clinicalContext: DKA patient with profound metabolic acidosis (pH 7.10, HCO3 8 mmol/L) recently intubated.
learnerInput: The patient requires a high minute ventilation matching their high pre-intubation spontaneous respiratory drive to prevent catastrophic worsening of acidemia.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Severe metabolic acidosis relies on respiratory compensation; under-ventilating a DKA patient results in severe mixed acidosis and circulatory collapse.

clinicalContext: Patient on VC 450 mL, Pplat 22, PEEP 5. ABG shows pH 7.48, PaCO2 31 mmHg, PaO2 95 mmHg.
learnerInput: The patient has respiratory alkalosis from mild hyperventilation. I will decrease the set respiratory rate by 2-4 breaths/min to allow PaCO2 to normalize toward 40 mmHg.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Alveolar ventilation is directly proportional to tidal volume minus dead space times respiratory rate; reducing rate increases PaCO2.

clinicalContext: Severe COPD on VC with dynamic hyperinflation and rising auto-PEEP. Expiratory flow does not reach zero.
learnerInput: I will lower the set respiratory rate because a slower rate blows off more carbon dioxide per minute.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Lowering rate is correct to lengthen expiratory time and reduce gas trapping, but lowering rate decreases minute ventilation and does not blow off more CO2.

clinicalContext: Patient with high Ppeak (38) and normal Pplat (20) on VC with square flow waveform.
learnerInput: I will change from square flow to decelerating ramp because decelerating ramp improves alveolar recruitment in stiff lungs.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Decelerating flow lowers peak airway pressure by reducing peak flow at end-inspiration, but normal Pplat indicates lung compliance is normal.

clinicalContext: Ventilated patient with acute hypoxemia (SpO2 86%). FiO2 is 0.5. Clear CXR, sudden drop in EtCO2, tachycardia.
learnerInput: I will order a CT pulmonary angiogram because the sudden drop in EtCO2 means the endotracheal tube has slipped into the esophagus.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: CTPA is indicated for suspected pulmonary embolism (high alveolar dead space lowering EtCO2), not esophageal intubation.

clinicalContext: Post-op abdominal surgery patient with low lung compliance and atelectasis on PEEP 5.
learnerInput: I will increase PEEP from 5 to 10 cmH2O because higher PEEP increases airway resistance to push secretions out.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Increasing PEEP recruits collapsed alveoli and increases FRC, not by increasing airway resistance.

clinicalContext: Ventilator circuit shows massive condensate pooling in the tubing, with water-hammer fluttering on the flow scalar.
learnerInput: I will drain the water trap because condensate makes the oxygen molecules too heavy to diffuse into the blood.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Circuit condensate causes flow artifact and auto-triggering, not impairment of molecular diffusion.

clinicalContext: Patient with acute respiratory acidosis (pH 7.22, PaCO2 62) on PSV with Vt 280 mL.
learnerInput: I will increase pressure support from 8 to 14 cmH2O because pressure support directly expands the pulmonary capillary blood volume.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Pressure support increases transpulmonary pressure to deliver a larger tidal volume and augment alveolar ventilation.

clinicalContext: ARDS patient on FiO2 0.8 and PEEP 10 with SpO2 92%.
learnerInput: I will increase PEEP to 14 cmH2O so that I can wean the FiO2, because high FiO2 causes hypothermia.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: PEEP titration allows FiO2 reduction to prevent hyperoxic lung injury and absorption atelectasis, not hypothermia.

clinicalContext: Patient on VC experiencing double-triggering as they take deep spontaneous inspiratory efforts.
learnerInput: I will increase the set tidal volume because double-triggering means the patient has stopped breathing spontaneously.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Double-triggering represents patient-ventilator dyssynchrony from flow hunger or insufficient inspiratory time, indicating active spontaneous drive.

clinicalContext: Intubated asthmatic on VC with high Ppeak (45), Pplat (32), auto-PEEP 12 cmH2O, BP 82/50.
learnerInput: The patient has severe expiratory airflow limitation and gas trapping. To relieve this, I will add 10 cmH2O of extrinsic PEEP to push the trapped gas through the airways.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: The recognition of airflow limitation and air trapping is sound, but in passive flow-limited asthma, adding extrinsic PEEP increases total PEEP and worsens hyperinflation.

clinicalContext: Moderate ARDS with PaO2 62 on FiO2 0.7, Pplat 26 on Vt 6 mL/kg PBW, PEEP 8.
learnerInput: Oxygenation is inadequate due to shunt in collapsed dorsal alveoli. I will increase tidal volume from 380 mL to 650 mL to open up the atelectatic units.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Recognizing shunt from atelectasis is sound, but increasing tidal volume causes volutrauma; recruitment should be achieved with PEEP or proning.

clinicalContext: COPD patient with acute respiratory acidosis on NIV (IPAP 12, EPAP 4, pH 7.28, PaCO2 58).
learnerInput: The patient is hypoventilating with hypercapnia. I will increase EPAP to 10 cmH2O while keeping IPAP at 12 cmH2O.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Recognizing hypercapnia is sound, but narrowing the pressure support (IPAP - EPAP) from 8 to 2 reduces tidal volume and worsens hypercapnia.

clinicalContext: Patient on VC 450 mL, RR 18, Ppeak 28, Pplat 26. MAP 85. PaCO2 46.
learnerInput: Plateau pressure reflects alveolar distension. Because plateau is 26, the lung is dangerously overdistended, so I must reduce PEEP to 0 immediately.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Recognizing that Pplat reflects alveolar pressure is sound, but Pplat of 26 is below the safe threshold of 30 cmH2O; zero PEEP promotes de-recruitment.

clinicalContext: Neuromuscular patient with Guillain-Barre on PSV with tachypnea (RR 34) and small Vt (180 mL).
learnerInput: The patient has severe diaphragm weakness causing rapid shallow breathing. I will administer high-dose fentanyl to slow down their breathing rate.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Recognizing neuromuscular diaphragm weakness is sound, but opioid sedation will suppress drive and cause hypercapnic arrest.

clinicalContext: Hypoxemic patient with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema on BiPAP (IPAP 14, EPAP 6). BP 160/95.
learnerInput: Pulmonary venous congestion is flooding alveoli. I will decrease EPAP to 2 cmH2O to help fluid drain back into the systemic circulation.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Understanding pulmonary congestion is sound, but positive intrathoracic pressure (EPAP) reduces LV afterload and venous return; lowering EPAP worsens cardiogenic edema.

clinicalContext: Severe ARDS patient. Driving pressure is 19 cmH2O. Pplat 32, PEEP 13.
learnerInput: High driving pressure correlates strongly with increased mortality in ARDS. Therefore, I will decrease PEEP from 13 to 4 cmH2O while keeping Vt the same.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: High driving pressure is indeed associated with mortality, but dropping PEEP to 4 in severe ARDS induces severe alveolar collapse and can further worsen compliance and driving pressure.

clinicalContext: Patient on mechanical ventilation with sudden rise in Ppeak to 48 cmH2O while Pplat remains stable at 20 cmH2O.
learnerInput: Airway resistance has increased acutely. Because the problem is in the airway, the patient needs emergency bilateral tube thoracostomies.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Recognizing acute resistive elevation is correct, but tension pneumothorax increases both Pplat and Ppeak; airway obstruction (tube kinking/mucus) needs suction/clearing, not chest drains.

clinicalContext: Intubated patient with deteriorating ABG. Ventilator alarm sounds.
learnerInput: The vent is acting up. We should fix it.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Unclear statement without specific physiological observation or proposed action requires clarification.

clinicalContext: Post-extubation patient with mild stridor and tachypnea.
learnerInput: Let's change something on the machine.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Completely ambiguous intervention without identifying the clinical issue.

clinicalContext: Septic shock with acute lung injury on VC.
learnerInput: Maybe turn the dials up a bit?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Ambiguous request with no specified parameter or clinical rationale.

clinicalContext: Patient triggering asynchronous breaths on PSV.
learnerInput: The waveform looks kind of weird.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Vague observation without specifying which scalar, phase of respiration, or dyssynchrony pattern.

clinicalContext: Arterial blood gas shows metabolic acidosis with compensatory tachypnea.
learnerInput: Gas looks bad. What do you think?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Nondescript evaluation requiring learner to articulate specific acid-base or oxygenation disorder.

clinicalContext: Asthmatic with severe auto-PEEP (14 cmH2O) and persistent expiratory flow. Monitored Ppeak 42, Pplat 28.
learnerInput: I am 100% certain that increasing the respiratory rate from 16 to 24 will cure this problem by giving more ventilation.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: High confidence in an intervention that drastically shortens expiratory time and exacerbates dynamic hyperinflation warrants Level 3 teaching.

clinicalContext: Patient on VC experiencing severe patient-ventilator dyssynchrony with high airway pressures.
learnerInput: I am absolutely sure that immediately paralyzing this patient with rocuronium is the first step before checking the endotracheal tube.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Paralysis without assessing tube patency or mechanical airway obstruction is a critical safety mistake.

clinicalContext: ARDS patient with driving pressure of 22 cmH2O.
learnerInput: Without question, driving pressure has zero clinical significance as long as SpO2 is above 90%.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Driving pressure is the strongest mechanical ventilator predictor of mortality in ARDS.

clinicalContext: Patient with left-sided tension pneumothorax, tracheal deviation, and hypotension.
learnerInput: I am completely certain that the first thing to do is order an urgent CT scan of the chest.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Tension pneumothorax is an immediate clinical diagnosis requiring prompt needle decompression, not delayed imaging.

clinicalContext: Patient with PaO2 55 on FiO2 1.0 due to large right pulmonary artery clot (V/Q mismatch / shunt).
learnerInput: Increasing FiO2 to 1.5 with high pressure oxygen therapy will definitely resolve an anatomical shunt.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: True physiological shunt is refractory to supplementary oxygen because blood bypasses ventilated alveoli entirely.

clinicalContext: ARDS on VC with Pplat 34 cmH2O and Vt 7.5 mL/kg PBW.
learnerInput: Just taking a wild guess, maybe we should drop the tidal volume to 6 mL/kg to lower the plateau pressure below 30?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Underconfident learner identified the correct target and rationale.

clinicalContext: Obstructive patient on flow-time scalar with expiratory tail.
learnerInput: I could be totally wrong here, but looking at that expiratory curve, does flow fail to hit zero before the breath starts?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Accurate identification of incomplete expiration presented with low confidence.

clinicalContext: Patient on BiPAP with CO2 retention on IPAP 12 / EPAP 6.
learnerInput: Shot in the dark: should we raise the IPAP to increase the pressure support gradient and blow off more CO2?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Correctly identifies that expanding pressure support delta augments tidal volume and ventilation.

clinicalContext: Patient on PSV with auto-triggering caused by small cardiac oscillations.
learnerInput: Not really sure, but maybe the flow trigger threshold is too sensitive and picking up heartbeats?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Correct diagnosis of cardiogenic auto-triggering.

clinicalContext: Asthma case step 1: Ppeak is 40 cmH2O. Expiratory flow incomplete.
learnerInput: The peak pressure is high so I will increase the respiratory rate to give more ventilation.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: First occurrence of rate-increase misconception in air trapping.

clinicalContext: Asthma case step 2: Ppeak has risen to 46 cmH2O. Patient more tachycardic.
learnerInput: Still under-ventilated, so I will raise the rate even higher to 24.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Second occurrence of air-trapping rate misconception.

clinicalContext: Asthma case step 3: Patient now hypotensive with severe auto-PEEP.
learnerInput: I need to increase the set rate again to treat this acidosis.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Third consecutive failure on same mechanism triggers Level 3 worked teaching.

clinicalContext: ARDS step 1: Pplat is 34 cmH2O.
learnerInput: Pplat 34 is fine as long as Ppeak is under 50.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Plateau pressure, not peak pressure, drives alveolar overdistension.

clinicalContext: ARDS step 2: Pplat increases to 36 cmH2O.
learnerInput: Ppeak is 44, so we still have headroom before reaching 50.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Persistent reliance on Ppeak threshold rather than Pplat.

clinicalContext: ARDS step 3: Pneumothorax risk high, Pplat 38.
learnerInput: Peak is 48, so we are still safe under 50.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Third consecutive error triggers direct worked explanation on Pplat and driving pressure.

clinicalContext: COPD NIV step 1: PaCO2 is 60, IPAP 12, EPAP 4.
learnerInput: I will increase EPAP to 8 to clear CO2.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Raising EPAP without IPAP reduces pressure support and ventilation.

clinicalContext: COPD NIV step 2: PaCO2 rises to 68.
learnerInput: CO2 is higher so I will increase EPAP further to 10.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Second occurrence of equating EPAP with ventilation.

clinicalContext: COPD NIV step 3: Severe acidosis pH 7.20.
learnerInput: Let's increase EPAP to 12.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Third consecutive occurrence warrants Level 3 direct worked explanation of delta PS.

clinicalContext: Oxygen toxicity step 1: SpO2 100% on FiO2 1.0.
learnerInput: Leave FiO2 at 1.0 because more oxygen is always safer.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Hyperoxia causes absorption atelectasis and free radical injury.

clinicalContext: Oxygen toxicity step 2: PaO2 is 280 mmHg.
learnerInput: High PaO2 is great reserve, keep FiO2 at 1.0.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Failure to titrate down hyperoxia.

clinicalContext: Oxygen toxicity step 3: Patient on FiO2 1.0 for 24 hours.
learnerInput: FiO2 1.0 has no harms, keep it there.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Third consecutive failure triggers Level 3 worked teaching on target SpO2 92-96%.

clinicalContext: Learner types intention to lower tidal volume to protect the lung, but changes ventilator setting from 420 mL to 550 mL.
learnerInput: I want to apply lung protection so I dialed the tidal volume up to 550 mL.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Action of increasing tidal volume directly contradicts stated intention of lung protection.

clinicalContext: Learner intends to lengthen expiratory time in severe obstruction, but increases set respiratory rate from 14 to 26.
learnerInput: I need to give the patient more time to exhale so I increased the rate to 26.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Increasing respiratory rate shortens the total cycle time and shortens expiratory time.

clinicalContext: Learner states patient is severely hypoxic on FiO2 0.8, but dials FiO2 down to 0.4.
learnerInput: Patient has critical hypoxemia so I decreased FiO2 to 0.4.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Weaning oxygen in acute severe hypoxemia contradicts stated goal.

clinicalContext: Learner states patient has elevated PaCO2 and needs more ventilation, but switches ventilator mode to CPAP with PS 0.
learnerInput: The patient is retaining CO2 so I turned off all pressure support.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Eliminating pressure support in a fatiguing patient worsens hypoventilation.

clinicalContext: Asthma case with hidden probe 'dynamic hyperinflation'. Flow-time curve does not reach zero. Learner asks: 'Why is the pressure rising?'
learnerInput: Can you give me a hint about why the airway pressures are creeping up?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Tutor must direct attention to the end-expiratory flow on the scalar without naming auto-PEEP or dynamic hyperinflation.

clinicalContext: Tension pneumothorax hidden probe. High Ppeak and Pplat with sudden hypotension. Learner asks: 'What is happening?'
learnerInput: What is going on with the patient? Can you tell me the diagnosis?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Tutor must focus on acute compliance drop and hemodynamic collapse without naming pneumothorax.

clinicalContext: Endotracheal tube cuff leak hidden probe. Low exhaled tidal volume with audible leak.
learnerInput: Why is the exhaled volume smaller than the set volume?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Prompt learner to check for circuit and airway circuit continuity.

clinicalContext: Severe ARDS hidden probe. Low compliance.
learnerInput: Give me a hint on what setting to change.
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Guide learner to evaluate the driving pressure and plateau pressure without revealing target settings.

clinicalContext: Mainstem intubation hidden probe. Right lung hyperinflated, left absent breath sounds.
learnerInput: What could cause high peak and plateau pressure with unilateral chest rise?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Guide learner to compare bilateral physical findings.

clinicalContext: Secretions blocking airway hidden probe. Sawtooth pattern on flow-volume loop.
learnerInput: Why does the flow curve look jagged?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Prompt learner to consider physical obstructions creating turbulent oscillating airflow.

clinicalContext: Patient biting the ETT hidden probe. Sudden high Ppeak, normal Pplat on hold.
learnerInput: Ppeak jumped to 50 cmH2O suddenly. Why?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Direct learner to inspect the mouth and circuit for external mechanical narrowing.

clinicalContext: Ventilator dyssynchrony (ineffective triggering) hidden probe. Negative pressure deflections without triggered breath.
learnerInput: What are those small dips in the airway pressure waveform during expiration?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Prompt learner to analyze whether the patient's inspiratory effort reaches the trigger threshold.

clinicalContext: Intubated patient experiencing bronchospasm on mechanical ventilation.
learnerInput: How does inhaled ipratropium bromide work compared to albuterol at a cellular level?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Albuterol is a beta-2 adrenergic agonist (cAMP-mediated relaxation); ipratropium is a muscarinic antagonist (blocks acetylcholine-mediated bronchoconstriction).

clinicalContext: Post-cardiac arrest patient on ventilator.
learnerInput: Why do targeted temperature management protocols recommend avoiding hyperventilation?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Hypocapnia induces cerebral vasoconstriction, decreasing cerebral blood flow and aggravating secondary ischemic brain injury.

clinicalContext: ARDS patient being evaluated for ECMO candidacy.
learnerInput: What is the physiological difference between venovenous (VV) and venoarterial (VA) ECMO in gas exchange?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: VV ECMO provides respiratory support (oxygenation and decarboxylation) in series with the native heart; VA ECMO provides both cardiac and respiratory support in parallel.

clinicalContext: Moderate ARDS with PaO2/FiO2 140 mmHg on PEEP 10.
learnerInput: Should we use high PEEP or low PEEP for this moderate ARDS patient?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Meta-analyses of ALVEOLI/LOVS/EXPRESS trials showed a mortality benefit for higher PEEP in moderate-to-severe ARDS (P/F < 200), though individual trials were neutral.

clinicalContext: Early severe ARDS (P/F 80).
learnerInput: Does continuous neuromuscular blockade with cisatracurium reduce mortality in early severe ARDS?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: The ACURASYS trial found 90-day mortality benefit with 48 hours of cisatracurium in severe ARDS; the larger ROSE trial with lighter sedation targets found no mortality difference.

clinicalContext: ARDS patient being ventilated with conservative fluid management.
learnerInput: What is the evidence regarding conservative versus liberal fluid management in ARDS?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: The ARDSNet FACTT trial demonstrated conservative fluid management improved ventilator-free days and ICU stay without increasing non-pulmonary organ failure, but without significant mortality reduction.

clinicalContext: Severe acute exacerbation of COPD failing standard medical therapy.
learnerInput: Is non-invasive ventilation superior to upfront invasive mechanical ventilation in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure from COPD?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Extensive randomized trial evidence and Cochrane reviews support first-line NIV for acute hypercapnic COPD exacerbations, reducing intubation rates and mortality.

clinicalContext: Patient on mechanical ventilation ready for weaning assessment.
learnerInput: Is a T-piece spontaneous breathing trial or low-level pressure support trial superior for predicting extubation success?
keyPhysiologicalPoint: Recent trials (e.g. Subira et al. JAMA 2019) show pressure support SBTs increase extubation success compared to T-piece, but ongoing debate exists regarding post-extubation fatigue.
